item.text: {"text":"GRU4Rec’s official implementation recommends cross-entropy or BPR-max over ordinary BPR/TOP1 because the latter suffer vanishing gradients. BPR-max emphasizes high-scoring negatives through softmax weights and adds negative-score regularization; sampled cross-entropy provides a useful competing objective, with logQ correction available for nonuniform sampling. Neither is established as universally superior. [Official GRU4Rec](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec), [original ranking-loss paper](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf). A 2024 sequential-recommendation study compared random, popularity, in-batch, mixed and adaptive sampling: results depended on dataset popularity structure, and aggregate accuracy concealed substantial head/mid/tail differences. Popularity-based sampling sometimes improved balance while reducing overall accuracy. [Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276).\n\nHarder negatives can also be unobserved positives. Hard-BPR (2024) modifies the ranking objective specifically to reduce false-negative damage during dynamic hard sampling; its evidence comes from implicit collaborative filtering, so transfer to GRU4Rec remains a hypothesis. [Hard-BPR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276). For this task, a defensible experiment is separate trials of one GRU4Rec per category using sampled cross-entropy versus regularized BPR-max, followed by controlled changes to negative count and uniform/popularity sampling. Exclude padding, the current target and known training positives from negative pools; this removes known collisions but cannot identify every false negative. Test moderate hardness before aggressively mining the highest-scoring items. These are experimental recommendations, not demonstrated Electronics improvements: retain seed 42, fixed splits and training limits, and select exclusively by the pinned four-category macro validation HR@10. Training margins alone cannot establish better recommendation ranking."}
